en-rd-a.title: A
en-rd-a.text:
Oak Mill Kitchen Open House

The long tables where mill workers once had lunch now belong to a community kitchen. On Saturday, May 15, our cooks will open their doors and share some of the things they make here each week. Admission to the building is free. Visitors can look around the main room and see what is growing in the kitchen garden throughout the day.

Fresh Pasta  |  9:30–10:10  |  $6
Work a piece of dough with your hands, roll it flat, and learn to fill and fold it. We will send you home with the recipe so you can try a different filling in your own kitchen. Ages eight and up.

Lunchbox Lab  |  10:45–11:30  |  $9
Put together a lunch from a table of roasted vegetables, sauces, and fresh breads. The cook will explain how to pack a meal so that the bread stays fresh until you eat it. Bring a reusable container for the lunch you make. Ages ten and up.

Bread Shapes  |  13:15–14:00  |  $9
Make a small loaf from dough prepared that morning. Once your loaf goes into the oven, you can watch through the glass and see how the shape changes as it bakes. Ages twelve and up.

Baker at Work  |  15:00–15:35  |  Free
Watch our baker turn out a batch of rolls for the community supper. This is a demonstration for all ages, with seats behind the kitchen barrier.

Planning your visit
Workshop fees are per participant and include ingredients. Anyone under fourteen must have an adult stay with them. Adults who only watch can come along for free. Book workshops online and check in at the side desk at least ten minutes before the start. After that deadline, we offer any unclaimed places to visitors on the waiting list. You can put your name on that list at the side desk on the day of the event. For the demonstration, simply arrive at the barrier a few minutes early.

en-rd-b.title: B
en-rd-b.text:
I loved the board at the back of the bicycle shop on Pine Street. It showed how many donated bikes each volunteer had repaired that Saturday. On my fourth Saturday I counted five marks beside my name. Mr. Vega, who ran the shop, drew a star there in chalk. I went to wash my hands and came back past the board, although there was a shorter way to the door.

My fifth bike, a blue one with a new bell, was waiting for a boy named Eli. When he came in, I rang the bell to show him how it sounded. He smiled but stayed where he was, holding the strap of a long black case. Mr. Vega asked about it. “My trumpet,” Eli said. “I'm supposed to go straight from school to rehearsal. Do you think it'll fit on this?”

I was about to tell him to carry the case on his back when he lifted it, and I saw the narrow strap pull tight against his shoulder. Mr. Vega pointed to a red bicycle we were keeping for spare parts. Its rear rack (架子) was long enough to take the case. We moved the rack over to the blue bike and added two broad straps. When I started to fasten the second one, Mr. Vega handed it to Eli. “Give it a try,” he said. Eli took both straps off and put them on again. Then he did it once more, quicker this time.

Outside, the black case made the bike look larger than before. Eli rode slowly to the corner, turned, and came back with his feet still on the pedals. “Does the shop close soon?” he called. “I want to try it on the hill.” I stood in the doorway until he disappeared around the corner again.

When I came in the following Saturday, I put a pencil beside the pickup sheet. There was a blank space after each name, just wide enough for a few words. The first visitor looked down at my pencil and then at the bicycle by the door. I asked her where she would ride and what she needed to carry.

en-rd-c.title: C
en-rd-c.text:
A woodland can turn green while much of its recovery remains out of sight. New leaves are easy to see, but finding out whether small animals have returned to the soil usually involves taking samples and sorting through them by hand. Since many of those animals make faint sounds as they move, researchers in South Australia asked whether recordings might offer another way to follow the recovery that takes place underground.

At Mount Bold, the team worked in patches of original grassy woodland, patches where native plants had been put back, and patches that had been cleared and left without replanting. They recorded at each kind of site by inserting a metal probe (探针) that could pick up vibrations, and they also recorded equal volumes of soil inside a box lined with material that helped keep outside noise out. Since the probe might pick up vibrations from different distances in the field, the box gave the team a more consistent space in which to record. Once they had finished recording in the box, they searched through the soil and counted the animals they found, yielding an independent set of observations for comparison.

One of the team's measures tracked how much the strength of sound varied from moment to moment across a range of frequencies. On this measure, recordings from the original and replanted patches scored higher than those from the cleared patches, both in the ground and in the box. When the team compared the results with the hand counts, they found a link between greater sound variation and a greater variety of animals.

Even in the same patch of woodland, a change in soil moisture could <u>muddy</u> a comparison between two recordings. A drop in the score after rain, for instance, could reflect a change in how vibrations travel through the soil, so the score alone gives little reason to conclude that some of the animals have gone. Similarly, a recording offers a picture of only the brief period when the equipment was running, and animals that are less active at that hour may be hard to detect.

A practical use of the technique would be to take repeated readings under comparable conditions and follow up unusual results with direct checks. A recording at one location takes only minutes, so listening could help researchers decide where it is worth doing the slower work of looking for animals.

en-rd-d.title: D
en-rd-d.text:
Potholes (坑洼) are easy to report in a city with a service such as 311, which takes requests for local government services. A resident gives the location, and the request is passed on to the department responsible for repairs. A different question arises when officials make a map from those requests and use it to decide which neighborhoods need the largest share of repair work.

Consider two districts, each with one hundred holes of much the same size in its roads. Fifty of the holes in one district are reported to the city, while ten in the other district are reported. A map based solely on those reports will give the impression that the first district is in much poorer shape, though street crews would find the same number of holes in either place. Increasing access to the reporting system by itself may do little to close that gap. Even if filing a report took the same effort everywhere, residents might differ in how much they expected it to help.

A study of Houston compared residents' requests with records of potholes the city had filled on its own initiative. Those repairs offered another clue to where roads needed work, since crews could find holes that nobody had reported. In some areas with fewer economic advantages, the problem of potholes appeared more common on this measure even as requests from residents were less frequent. The repair records still offered an estimate, since they covered the streets the crews had reached in the course of their work. Because the records were grouped by area, the researchers could see a pattern across neighborhoods. Investigating why a particular person chose to file a request would have required a different kind of evidence.

Suppose a city reduces the time between a report and a repair, giving callers one more reason to use the service again. That is worth doing, and a city could meet its target for quick repairs while whole streets still waited for somebody to report a hole. To see how much work was going unnoticed, it could inspect a sample of streets chosen independently of the requests. Crews could visit a rotating set of roads in every district, including districts that rarely send requests. The results would help direct repair crews to neglected roads, and officials could still take requests about particular holes as they came in. Faster repairs after a call are worth tracking, and the condition of the whole road network deserves a measure of its own.

en-rd-gap.title: Leaving a Note for Next Year's Team
en-rd-gap.text:
The morning after a school event, it is easy to remember where you found extra chairs or why somebody moved the welcome table. A year later, a new team may face the same decisions with none of that knowledge. [36] ______ It can be short enough to write while the chairs are still being put away.

Start with the plan you actually followed. [37] ______ For example, if the original floor plan showed a single line at the entrance, mark where you ended up making a second one. A copy of the plan with a few arrows can tell the next team more than a page of instructions.

Record why you made each change as well. The extra line may have worked because it kept people from blocking the stairs. [38] ______ If next year's event uses a different entrance, they will know to check for another route that must stay clear.

Some details are worth checking with someone who worked in a different part of the event. [39] ______ The welcome desk volunteers might have seen a steady flow while those handing out equipment had a line that barely moved. Put both observations in the note so next year's team can decide where to provide extra help.

[40] ______ Store the note with the plan and the equipment list where next year's organizers will already be looking. Give it a name that includes the event and the date, so later teams can find the right version.

options.A: People at different stations can have quite different views of how the day went.
options.B: This is a good time to compare the plan with one from another event.
options.C: Make any changes to the original plan visible on the page.
options.D: If a change worked well, recommend doing the same thing the following year.
options.E: That is when a brief note from this year's organizers can help.
options.F: Finally, make it easy for the new team to find your note.
options.G: Knowing the reason gives the next team something they can apply in a new place.
